https://www.planetf1.com/news/adrian-new.text: Adrian Newey observing in the Aston Martin garage Adrian Newey suggested that Lance Stroll ’s suspected rear suspension failure in Hungary was not related to the Aston Martin AMR26 upgrade package. Newey therefore described it as a “very unexpected” failure as Aston Martin begins its opening phase of developing the AMR26. Newey also confirmed that Honda is investigating the cause of vibrations, which were reported by Fernando Alonso, and could be seen on the data. In terms of pace, there were encouraging signs for Aston Martin. Adrian Newey addresses Stroll red flag and Honda review Want more PlanetF1.com coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust. There is a palpable buzz surrounding Aston Martin at the Hungaroring. At last, the team has sent its B-spec AMR26 into action. In terms of performance, it was a promising opening act. Alonso recorded a P13 finish in FP1. He slipped to 19th in the second hour of practice, but to be right in the mix with Cadillac remains a marked step forward. It was a more frustrating Friday on Lance Stroll’s side of the garage. Stroll triggered the red flags when he spun out of FP1. Aston Martin reported a suspected rear suspension failure. Stroll did not appear in FP2, as extensive work continued on his car. Adrian Newey, Aston Martin team principal and design chief, addressed the situation in Friday’s team leaders’ press conference. The area of failure in question was not a part of Aston Martin’s 16-piece upgrade, Newey confirmed. “Everybody is feverishly trying to understand exactly what went wrong and what happened as we speak, and it’s only once we have an understanding that we can comment on what we do next,” Newey told PlanetF1.com and others. “The area involved was actually not being changed. We are short on spares because the cladding and so forth is different. So there are some minor changes in that area. In that sense it was very unexpected. “As I say, until we have an understanding, it’s difficult to comment further.” Newey was also quizzed on a couple of Alonso team radio snippets. Alonso was urged to stay away from the kerbs before Stroll’s incident. Alonso also flagged up engine vibrations down the main straight at one stage in FP1. Newey explained both situations, confirming that Honda has launched an investigation into Alonso’s report. “So the first question, staying away from the kerbs, that’s purely because we are acquiring aero data,” said Newey. “When you’re trying to acquire aero data, you don’t want the disruption of kerbs thrown in, the inconsistency that corrupts the data. “The oscillations, yes, that’s really a question for Honda. They can see it on the data, and they are working on the solution.” More on Aston Martin from PlanetF1.com Aston Martin confirms ‘different direction’ as $1million question answered Upgraded Honda engine set to debut in Hungaroring run Teething issues are inevitable with such a substantial development package. Honda will soon throw its hat in the ring. As reported by PlanetF1.com on Thursday, Honda is set to debut its upgraded engine in a Hungaroring filming day, during the week following the Hungarian Grand Prix. (@YourAnonTV) September 19, 2026 Germany: Scenarios for 1,000 wounded per day Perhaps the most characteristic example of the shifting climate is found in Germany . The Bundeswehr is now planning based on a scenario in which up to 1,000 wounded soldiers per day would need to be treated in the event of a major military clash on NATO 's eastern flank. German Surgeon General Ralf Hoffmann had stated that the country must be prepared for such a volume of casualties, with wounded personnel transferred from the front lines into German civilian hospitals. The Bundeswehr estimates that approximately 15,000 hospital beds might be required. In 2026 , preparation moved from theory into practice. In the exercise Medic Quadriga 2026 , more than 1,000 military personnel and hundreds of civilian agencies tested an entire casualty evacuation chain from Lithuania to Germany . The scenario involved military medical units, aviation assets, rescue services, and civilian hospitals. The official German rationale is that this represents defensive preparation for an Article 5 contingency. For Moscow , however, the picture is different: one of Europe's largest powers is now systematically organizing not merely the defense of its territory, but the medical support infrastructure for a large-scale war in Eastern Europe. Lithuania plans mass evacuation Even more telling is the case of Lithuania . In July 2026 , the government approved a detailed national population evacuation plan for military or civil crises. The plan estimates that approximately 75% of the population could evacuate danger zones using their own means, while state and municipal authorities would handle the evacuation of the remaining 25%, prioritizing children, the elderly, and individuals with disabilities. The plan does not pertain exclusively to war with Russia ; it covers broader military and civil emergencies. The timing, however, is difficult to separate from the unprecedented military activity in the Baltic region. Lithuania now sits on the front line of NATO 's eastern flank, hosting a permanent German military presence. In June , the newly formed German Panzerbrigade 45 conducted its first large-scale exercise at the Pabrade training grounds, involving roughly 2,900 troops and 800 vehicles from eight NATO countries. The brigade is expected to reach approximately 5,000 military and civilian personnel once it attains full operational capability. For NATO , this represents a reinforcement of deterrence. For Russia , it represents new permanent military infrastructure of the Alliance directly adjacent to its borders. The Baltic fills with military exercises In 2026 , military activity was not confined to Lithuania . In exercise Cold Response 26 , more than 32,000 military personnel from 14 NATO countries deployed primarily across Norway and Finland . In BALTOPS 2026 , approximately 6,000 troops from 15 allied nations trained in the Baltic Sea in anti-submarine warfare, air defense, amphibious operations, and mine countermeasures. Concurrently, Ramstein Flag 2026 mobilized more than 200 aircraft and aviation assets from up to 18 nations. Facing this mobilization, Belarus conducted its own exercises in September near the borders with Lithuania and Poland , involving mechanized and armored units, drones, and counter-sabotage training. Minsk characterized these activities as defensive. Thus, the classic «security dilemma» is established: each side frames its own moves as defensive while treating the corresponding actions of the adversary as potentially aggressive. The result is more troops, more armaments, and shorter distances between them. Finland's F-35s alter the equation Perhaps the most significant new factor lies even further north. On September 18, 2026 , the first two F-35A aircraft of the Finnish Air Force touched down at the Lapland Air Wing base in Rovaniemi . They were the first of a total of 64 F-35A fighters ordered by Finland to replace its fleet of F/A-18 Hornet aircraft. This represents a development of distinct geostrategic significance, explains Military Watch Magazine . Finland shares approximately 1,340 kilometers of common border with Russia , and following its accession to NATO in 2023 , this entire line became a Russia – NATO frontier. Now, one of the most advanced Western fighter platforms is entering that exact theater. The F-35 features low radar cross-section, advanced sensor suites, and intelligence-gathering and data-sharing capabilities, having been engineered for operations in contested environments featuring dense air defense systems. For Helsinki , the procurement represents the modernization of national defense. From the Russian strategic perspective, however, geography is decisive: advanced NATO stealth fighters will now operate from bases significantly closer to critical regions of northwestern Russia . The F-35 clearly won the Finnish tender The selection of the F-35 was no accident. In the HX Fighter Program competition, the fighter achieved a score of 4.47, whereas the next highest-ranking competitor reached 3.81. The then-Commander of the Finnish Air Force, Pasi Jokinen , had stated that the F-35 took or shared first place across all core evaluated mission sets. Finland will ultimately field a fleet of 64 Block 4 aircraft, equipped with modern air-to-air and air-to-ground precision munitions. This does not automatically imply that the aircraft have an offensive mission against Russia . It does mean, however, that the military balance in Northern Europe is shifting markedly. And in strategic calculus, the capabilities of a weapons system matter regardless of the declared intentions of the government deploying it. The nuclear question Here, an even more sensitive factor comes into view. The Finnish government has pursued legislative amendments to remove legal barriers to the import, transit, or possession of nuclear devices within the framework of national defense, NATO collective defense, or other defense cooperation. The F-35A is nuclear-certified in US service and capable of delivering the B61-12 thermonuclear bomb. This does not mean, however, that Finland has decided to host American nuclear weapons. On the contrary, President Alexander Stubb stated on September 14 that Finland does not intend to host nuclear weapons on its soil in peacetime, even as the nation integrates more deeply into European nuclear deterrence architectures. For Moscow , however, the issue is not limited to whether B61 bombs are physically present in Finland today. The altered legal framework and the deployment of nuclear-capable F-35 jets establish a capability that previously did not exist to the same degree. Yet NATO maintains no Russian attack is imminent Here lies perhaps the greatest paradox. European governments discuss a Russian threat, organize mass evacuations, prepare hospitals for hundreds or thousands of wounded, deploy brigades to eastern borders, and procure cutting-edge military systems. Concurrently, a NATO official stated in late August that the Alliance sees no immediate threat of military attack against any of its members. Even the Estonian Foreign Intelligence Service assessed in February that it does not anticipate a Russian attack against a NATO member in the near future, although it warned that Moscow is reconstituting and expanding its military capacity. Russia , for its part, denies planning any attack against the Alliance. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov described claims of Russian preparations to attack NATO as «nonsense» in December 2025 , reiterating past denials by Vladimir Putin . Western governments counter that the absence of an immediate threat today is no guarantee for the future, and that deterrence requires preparation before danger materializes. (@SprinterPress) September 18, 2026 Europe enters a new military era Regardless of which assessment proves accurate, one fact is difficult to dispute: Europe's military architecture is transforming at a speed unseen since the Cold War. Germany is preparing for 1,000 wounded per day. Lithuania has organized a state evacuation apparatus. German armored forces are permanently stationing in the Baltic . Tens of thousands of soldiers are drilling across Northern Europe. And 64 F-35A fighters are gradually entering the Finnish Air Force. For European governments, all this represents an insurance policy against potential future hazards. Viewed from Moscow , however, the exact same reality can be read in reverse: NATO , which was once hundreds of kilometers away, has expanded to the Russian border, is bolstering permanent forces, and is stationing increasingly sophisticated weapons systems in the region. Thus emerges the greatest risk in contemporary European security: one side rearms out of fear of the other, and the other responds because it views that rearmament as a threat. As long as this dynamic persists, the distance between «deterrence» and direct military clash continues to shrink. Europe may maintain that it is preparing so that war never happens. The reality, however, is that from the Baltic to the Arctic Circle , it is now militarily preparing as if such a conflict can no longer be discounted. Anti-Russian hysteria: They see hybrid attacks in the EU and «stealth mobilization» of 300,000 soldiers Furthermore, a climate of hysteria prevails in European capitals regarding the prospect that Russia is allegedly intensifying so-called «hybrid» operations against NATO member states. The same sources, however, appear cautious regarding the scenario of an overt, mass mobilization of 300,000 soldiers, emphasizing that for the time being, what is primarily recorded is the creation of the necessary mechanisms in the event that a relevant political decision is taken. Concurrently, reports indicate that Russia is stepping up recruitment efforts, seeking new personnel even among citizens facing financial or legal difficulties. At the same time, European leaders warn of an escalation in hybrid threats, ranging from cyberattacks and sabotage to drone incursions and airspace violations. In an interview, Edgars Rinkēvičs noted that if Russia simultaneously launched multiple missiles against a NATO state, existing interception capabilities in several nations could prove inadequate. Simultaneously, he emphasized that drone technology and contemporary aerial warfare are developing at breakneck speed. The Chair of the NATO Military Committee, Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone , stated that the Alliance is ready in terms of structures, personnel, and weapons systems, underscoring that the primary goal is deterrence: a potential adversary must recognize that the costs of an attack would far exceed any gains. References to plans spanning roughly 4,000 pages point to the new regional defense plans approved at the Vilnius Summit in 2023 . NATO characterizes them as the most comprehensive collective defense blueprints since the Cold War, featuring concrete provisions detailing how allied forces would move and deploy in the event of a crisis. At the time, the Alliance had also announced that these plans would be supported by approximately 300,000 troops at high readiness. https://www.politico.eu/article/europes-.text: Europe’s biggest political family is already preparing its 2029 election strategy to win back voters from the far right — even as its own members split over whether to work with those parties and how far to follow them on policy. The center-right European People’s Party chair, Manfred Weber, internally launched a “Win2029” task force two weeks ago. The main goal of the group will be to develop an attractive enough policy platform to take on the far right at the polls in three years’ time. But interviews and internal meeting records reveal deepening disagreements over cooperation with far-right groups and how closely to align with them on migration, climate and social issues. Advertisement “The main polarization across the continent in many national elections, and certainly in the European election 2029 … will be the anti-European populists against the EPP parties,” said EPP vice-chair and Romanian prime minister nominee Siegfried Mureșan. Anything beyond the “battle” between EPP and the far right “will be of secondary importance,” echoed the conservative group’s spokesperson Pedro López de Pablo. “Because they are not in government, they can promise the earth. Faced with that kind of rhetoric, we need to think of which alternatives we can offer to the people.” Siegfried Mureșan participates in a meeting in Brussels on June 26, 2025. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images With the European Parliament not yet halfway through its current term, the task force marks an unusually early start to the EPP’s 2029 election preparations — and underscores the urgency party leaders feel as far-right parties gain ground across the bloc. Led by Spanish MEP Esteban González Pons, the task force will help draft the party’s final electoral program. Talks are due to start at an October retreat in Sicily and continue through next spring’s EPP congress in Rome. EPP lawmakers are already wrestling with the choice ahead. “This is the political history, the historical dilemma EPP needs to decide — it needs to be clear and it needs be truthful for the voters, are we center right or are we another right-wing party? ” said Finnish EPP lawmaker Sirpa Pietikäinen. Advertisement To deal or not to deal The divisions reflect different political realities across the party. In some countries, governing with the far right has become a political reality; in others, those parties remain the EPP’s main rivals and cooperation is a red line. Poles and Romanians oppose any alignment with the far right, while conservatives in Spain, Sweden, Finland, Denmark and the Netherlands have governed with them. German lawmakers are divided, as some in Berlin start questioning the firewall against Alternative for Germany (AfD) given its recent electoral successes. Yet most German EPP members in Brussels remain opposed. “There has always been that discussion within the party: Whether we should put content first, or the centrist platform first,” said Finnish EPP delegation chief Mika Aaltola. Mika Aaltola sits in the European Parliament in Brussels on July 16, 2025. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images Meeting notes from the past six months show the EPP attempting to maintain its firewall in the Parliament, with lawmakers repeatedly instructed to reject the far-right Patriots’ initiatives while backing similar proposals from the right-wing European Conservatives and Reformists, home to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. The EPP considers ECR an acceptable partner. To make an example of one of its lawmakers and quell criticism, the group went as far as to expel Slovenian MEP Branko Grims after he appeared at an event organized by the AfD. Yet the EPP cannot escape the temptation to go with far-right groups on sensitive issues where agreement with the Socialists and Democrats is harder to reach. Advertisement That happened recently on the EU’s long-term budget file, when a right-wing majority voted to strip green and gender criteria from spending oversight. EPP leaders had vowed to stick with the center but could not keep lawmakers in line, exposing a divide now spilling into day-to-day legislative battles. At its last plenary, the EPP group discussed how to pass a resolution on the migration crisis in Ceuta, the Spanish territory, after negotiations with the Socialists and Democrats collapsed. Two sets of internal notes seen by POLITICO show the strategy was to make the Patriots feel part of the process and get their vote by deliberately backing one of their amendments. A temporary migrant camp is set up at El Trampolín beach in Ceuta, Spain, where more than 2,000 migrants are estimated to be living, according to the latest figures on Sept. 24, 2026. | Manu Brabo/Getty Images The idea came from the Spanish delegation, which wanted a political win in Madrid. EPP leaders backed the plan, urging lawmakers to support the text whether or not the Patriots’ amendments passed. Migration tensions The EPP’s bigger challenge may be not whether to work with the far right, but whether to fight it on its issues or shift the political agenda onto its own terrain — and, in doing so, whether to move right to win back voters or stand their ground in the center. At the congress following the 2024 EU election, Weber made clear that he wanted to reshape the party’s “narrative” to regain support from voters tempted by far-right populists. That meant tougher migration policies, more deportations and rolling back green rules — positions that have only hardened since. Even as the EU’s Migration Pact introduced faster asylum and border procedures in June, and negotiators agreed on bloc-wide rules to speed up deportations, the EPP pushed for tougher measures. Advertisement At its Vienna political assembly that month, it called for more investment in Frontex, the EU’s coast guard agency, and easier returns at the bloc’s external border. Delegates also agreed to replace “irregular migration” with “illegal migration” throughout the text, adopting language more commonly associated with the far right, according to the confidential minutes. That migration strategy is raising eyebrows within the party. During a heated debate on political Islam in Europe in the same assembly, EPP Vice President and former Commissioner Mairead McGuinness warned colleagues “against conflating religious faith with political extremism,” calling for “a clear commitment to freedom of religion,” the minutes read. A French member of Frontex works at the cross-Channel terminal in Calais, France on July 25, 2024. | Bernard Barron/AFP via Getty Images German EPP lawmaker Dennis Radtke, who leads the party’s wing in charge of relations with trade unions, told POLITICO the party should avoid blaming the far right’s rise on migration alone. “Of course we have to ensure secure borders, no doubt about that, but to link the success of the extreme right in Europe only with the question of migration … I have doubts that this is the case,” he said. “The asylum seeker numbers are going down; the extreme right is still going up because a lot of social problems are not solved or even touched.” Culture wars As competitiveness and deregulation dominate the EPP’s response to Europe’s economic woes, some fear social and workers’ rights are being sidelined. Advertisement In February, the party’s workers’, seniors’ and women’s wings pushed a resolution calling for stronger social protections, skills and youth employment support. Austrian, Finnish, German and Swedish delegates came out against it, accusing it of being “poorly framed”, as “its focus on social justice sends the wrong signal given EPP priorities on competitiveness and productivity,” according to meeting minutes. Other lawmakers pushed back, arguing the party could not abandon the social dimension. The leadership postponed the vote, and the resolution quietly disappeared from the next meeting’s agenda. “It has not become easier,” said Radtke of trying to strengthen the EPP’s social focus. “If we are not willing to deliver on workers’ rights, on social issues, then we cannot claim to be Europe’s last people’s party.” Mairead McGuinness speaks during a press conference at the EU headquarters in Brussels on June 27, 2023. | Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP via Getty Images The far right’s culture wars are also reverberating inside the EPP, where longstanding tensions over feminism, gender and reproductive rights are shifting in favor of the conservative camp. In Parliament, the EPP has traditionally backed strong sexual and reproductive rights while allowing national delegations a free vote on abortion, said veteran gender equality MEP Pietikäinen. Now, as some delegations harden their positions, consensus is eroding and more issues — including gender budgeting, which examines how public spending affects women and men — are left to free votes. “Now it has been more difficult,” she said. A report on gender inequalities in health descended into pandemonium at an EPP group meeting last plenary, as Irish, Polish and Luxembourgish lawmakers urged colleagues to back it, while Spaniards called it “crazy” and Croatians denounced its “gender ideology” as “radical” and “extreme.” Advertisement The party’s vow to simplify EU legislation has also opened rifts, as lawmakers disagree on how far to scrap green laws. Its factions are divided over how far to weaken the combustion-engine phaseout, and how much to soften industry’s carbon emission restrictions under the Emissions Trading System, which puts a price on industrial emissions. The disputes expose the EPP’s central dilemma ahead of 2029: whether to harden its positions to win back voters from the far right or hold the center — a choice that risks deepening divisions among its national parties. Gabriel Gavin contributed reporting.

In a list of updated priorities released last month, Segal proposed an “external independent ombudsman” to monitor ABC and SBS coverage of the war in Gaza and to ensure publicly funded broadcasters were “held accountable to their own stated standards of accuracy and impartiality”. “Many in the Jewish community remain concerned that coverage they perceive as one-directional may contribute to a negative – and even hostile – view by audiences of those who support Israel, or have sympathy for it,” Segal said in her updated plan to combat antisemitism. The ABC said at the time its complaints process was “the most robust and transparent in the Australian media” and both broadcasters stated they were subject to external review by the Australian Communications and Media Authority (Acma). This week, government sources noted that Acma already acted as an external independent regulator that could investigate complaints if they needed to be escalated beyond the ABC and SBS ombudsmen. It was an evil “that tears at the fabric of our country … [and] puts the peaceful, free and equal society we cherish at risk”, they said. It is understood Labor could consider changes in response to recommendations from the royal commission into antisemitism that is scheduled to report in mid-December. The commission, headed by former high court judge Virginia Bell, was established after the antisemitic Bondi beach massacre in December 2025. “The government will soon receive the final report from the Royal Commission into Antisemitism and Social Cohesion,” Wells’ spokesperson said on Wednesday. “[It] will continue to work with the special envoy, the Jewish community and all Australians to combat antisemitism and strengthen our social cohesion.” Segal’s latest suggestion regarding the ABC and SBS received a mixed response a fortnight ago. Alex Ryvchin, the co-chief executive of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, welcomed Segal’s suggestions, warning meaningful oversight of coverage by public broadcasters could only be achieved “through external accountability”. Indeed, ensuring that the processes withstand fair scrutiny can only increase confidence.” The ABC ombudsman has previously investigated public complaints related to coverage of the Middle East and the war in Gaza, including the Israeli president’s visit to Australia and a press club address by the Israeli ambassador. ABC Alumni, which represents hundreds of former staff, has said that since October 2023 the ABC ombudsman has upheld four out of thousands of complaints of bias or inaccuracy relating to Middle East coverage. Acma, “to which dissatisfied complainants can appeal, has upheld none”, the group said in a statement, adding it was “outraged at the continued insistence by Jillian Segal … that the ABC and SBS, Australia’s most trusted news outlets, are contributing to antisemitism”. In her first report in mid-2025, Segal initially proposed the special envoy be given powers to monitor media organisations to encourage “accurate, fair and responsible reporting” to ensure impartiality and balance and to avoid “accepting false or distorted narratives”. She then told the royal commission into antisemitism in mid-2026 she wanted a new “oversight” committee that could give ABC and SBS coverage a “tick” or “guidance”. Segal told Senate estimates this week she was concerned about “the tone [and] the frequency of reporting about Gaza from the ABC”.
